strengths: Novel and elegant integration of multi-view diffusion models (specifically SV3D) for unsupervised 3D keypoint discovery, lifting the historical constraint of requiring synchronized and calibrated multi-view capture systems for training.
Strong quantitative performance on Human3.6M, outperforming single-view baselines and showing competitive results compared to some multi-view baselines.

Insightful feature design: the paper demonstrates that aggregating intermediate features directly from the multi-view diffusion U-net is superior to using features from other 2D vision foundation models (such as DINOv2 or CLIP).
Compelling downstream application of 3D object manipulation, showing how the discovered 3D keypoints can be used to rig and animate 3D Gaussians reconstructed from the same diffusion model.

Thorough evaluation, including extensive ablation studies (on viewpoints, backbones, number of keypoints, timesteps, and robustness to camera noise) and qualitative visualization on diverse in-the-wild datasets (DAVIS, AP-10K).
weaknesses: Significant computational overhead during inference: Table 6 reveals that running the multi-view diffusion model at inference takes ~12 seconds and consumes nearly 30GB of VRAM per image, which limits its practical use for real-time or resource-constrained applications.

Strong dependency on the generative quality of the multi-view diffusion model. As discussed in the failure cases, any inconsistency, flipping, or severe occlusion in the generated views directly translates to keypoint estimation errors.
The method still suffers from left-right ambiguity, which is a classic issue in unsupervised pose estimation but remains unresolved by this approach.

strengths: Novel and elegant framework that leverages multi-view diffusion models (such as SV3D) for both generating multi-view training supervision and extracting implicit 3D geometric features.
Strong quantitative and qualitative results, outperforming existing unsupervised single-view baselines on Human3.6M and demonstrating competitive performance with multi-view methods.
Excellent generalization performance to in-the-wild and out-of-domain categories (e.g., DAVIS, GSO, and AP-10K) without category-specific templates or human-specific priors.

Demonstrates an impressive downstream application of animatable 3D object generation by utilizing discovered keypoints and skeleton graphs to compute skinning weights on reconstructed 3D Gaussians/meshes.
weaknesses: Very high computational and memory cost during inference. As shown in Table 6, the diffusion stage requires nearly 12 seconds per iteration and nearly 30 GB of VRAM, limiting its applicability for real-time or resource-constrained scenarios.

Strong dependency on the generative quality of the multi-view diffusion backbone. As discussed in the failure cases, any inconsistency or occlusion artifacts produced by SV3D directly translate to errors in the predicted 3D keypoints.

The model still suffers from left-right/reflectional ambiguity (symmetrical flip) in self-supervised learning, as there is no explicit geometric constraint to resolve front-back or left-right orientation without manual priors.

strengths: Innovative integration of a pretrained multi-view diffusion model (SV3D) for unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint discovery, extending previous 2D-only diffusion prior keypoint methods to 3D.

Well-designed technical pipeline that leverages intermediate, multi-layer features from the diffusion model and lifts them into a 3D volumetric space, rather than treating the generative model solely as an image renderer.
Strong evaluation across diverse object categories (humans, birds, dogs) and robust generalization performance on out-of-distribution datasets like AP-10K, GSO, and DAVIS.
A creative downstream application is demonstrated, showing how the discovered keypoints can be used to construct animatable 3D models from a single image using Gaussian Frosting.
weaknesses: High computational cost and latency at inference time due to the reliance on the multi-view diffusion model (achieving only 0.08 iterations per second, as shown in Table 6), limiting its feasibility for real-time applications.

Heavy dependency on the quality of the generative backbone; errors, inconsistencies, or alignment failures in the multi-view diffusion generator propagate directly to the keypoint localization (as discussed in the failure cases).

Individual components (such as unprojection to 3D voxel grids, volumetric CNNs, and soft-argmax) are relatively standard blocks borrowed from prior works like BKinD-3D, making the primary contribution a system-level integration.

strengths: Innovative approach that bridges 2D multi-view diffusion models and unsupervised 3D keypoint discovery, effectively turning implicit generative priors into explicit, highly structured 3D volumetric representations.
Technically solid pipeline including multi-layer diffusion feature aggregation, 3D unprojection, and a self-supervised reconstruction-based training objective.
Strong quantitative results on Human3.6M, outperforming single-view baselines and showing competitive performance with methods trained on real multi-view data.

Outstanding zero-shot generalization capabilities across different domains, such as generalizing from humans to Google Scanned Objects, or dogs to wild animals (e.g., giraffes, rhinoceroses, and zebras).
Practical downstream application demonstrated by integrating the predicted keypoints with Gaussian Splatting (Gaussian Frosting) to achieve animatable 3D objects from a single image.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on the multi-view diffusion model's generation quality, meaning any geometric inconsistencies or artifacts in the generated views (e.g., for very complex or rare poses) will directly affect the keypoint accuracy.
High computational and inference cost due to the necessity of running multiple denoising steps to extract intermediate diffusion features.
Limited architectural details provided for the reconstruction network in Section 3.3; a more detailed description of how the appearance features and edge maps are fused would enhance reproducibility.

strengths: Innovative integration of pretrained multi-view diffusion models (SV3D) to supervise and power unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint estimation.
Eliminates the requirement of multi-view capture systems or calibrated multi-view training data, allowing training with only collections of unconstrained single-view images.

Demonstrates strong generalization capabilities, transferring effectively from synthetic/controlled datasets (Human3.6M, Stanford Dogs) to challenging in-the-wild and out-of-domain scenarios (DAVIS, GSO, AP-10K).
Presents a complete pipeline for a practical downstream application, showing how discovered 3D keypoints can be used to construct and animate 3D rigged models from a single image.
Comprehensive quantitative evaluation on Human3.6M, showing superior performance compared to previous unsupervised monocular baselines, and competitive results even against some multi-view methods.
weaknesses: High computational cost at inference time: Extracting intermediate features from the diffusion U-Net requires multiple denoising steps, which restricts the pipeline from running in real-time. A quantitative breakdown of inference latency/FLOPs would make this clearer.

Strong dependency on the generative quality of the multi-view diffusion model (SV3D-p). In cases of highly articulated or uncommon poses where SV3D fails to generate consistent views, the quality of both feature extraction and supervision will degrade significantly.

Lack of quantitative evaluation on the animal datasets (Stanford Dogs or AP-10K) to objectively measure the accuracy of animal pose estimation, relying instead primarily on qualitative visualizations.
Clarity on camera parameters: It would be helpful to explicitly explain how the camera projection matrices $P_k$ are determined/sampled during single-image inference.

strengths: Innovative use of multi-view diffusion priors: Leveraging pretrained multi-view diffusion models (like SV3D) both to synthesize self-supervision signals (novel views) and as a robust 3D feature extractor is a creative and promising solution to the highly under-constrained monocular 3D keypoint discovery problem.

Promising unsupervised performance: The proposed method successfully learns 3D keypoints from single-view image collections without requiring manual 3D annotations or calibrated multi-view camera rigs during training. It outperforms existing single-view unsupervised baselines on Human3.6M.

Downstream applicability: The integration of the estimated 3D keypoints with Gaussian Frosting to generate animatable 3D objects from a single image is a practical application that showcases the utility of the discovered structures.

Qualitative generalization: Shows visually compelling generalization results on out-of-distribution categories (e.g., Google Scanned Objects, different animal species in AP-10K) and in-the-wild datasets (DAVIS).
weaknesses: High inference computational cost: Since the model relies on extracting intermediate features from a multi-view diffusion model, it requires running a multi-step denoising process (from $t=T$ down to $\tau=500$) for every single input image at test time. This makes the method extremely slow and computationally expensive compared to standard feed-forward keypoint estimators. The paper should provide quantitative metrics on inference time, FLOPS, or GPU latency.

Incomplete quantitative evaluation on animal datasets: The authors introduce the Stanford Dogs dataset in Section 4.1 and discuss training on it in Section 4.3. However, no quantitative evaluation (such as keypoint transfer accuracy or PCK/MPJPE on Stanford Dogs or AP-10K) is provided. Ground-truth 2D/3D landmarks are available for these datasets, and a quantitative comparison against other unsupervised animal keypoint discovery methods would significantly strengthen the paper.

Sensitivity to generative consistency: The framework is heavily dependent on the quality and multi-view consistency of the underlying diffusion model (SV3D-p). When the diffusion model produces physical or geometric inconsistencies (e.g., for complex poses, self-occlusions, or highly out-of-domain shapes), the reconstructed 3D volume features will likely degrade. An analysis of how robust the keypoint estimation is to different levels of generation quality is missing.

Lack of hyperparameter analysis (e.g., diffusion timestep $\tau$): The choice of extraction timestep $\tau = 500$ is crucial, as intermediate diffusion features at different timesteps represent varying levels of semantic layout vs. fine-grained texture. The paper lacks an ablation study on the choice of $\tau$ to justify this decision.
Minor presentation issues: There are minor spelling typos in the figures, such as "3D keypionts" instead of "3D keypoints" in Figures 4 and 6.
